S P E C I A L I S S U E A R T I C L E
‘Towards a Global Pact for the Environment’: International
environmental law's factual, technical and (unmentionable)
normative gaps
Duncan French
| Louis J. Kotzé
Correspondence
Emails: Dfrench@lincoln.ac.uk;
Louis.Kotze@nwu.ac.za
A key feature of the 2018 United Nations (UN) General Assembly Resolution
‘Towards a Global Pact for the Environment’ is the preparation of a technical and
evidence‐based report by the UN Secretary‐General that identifies and assesses pos-
sible gaps in international environmental law (IEL) and environment‐related instru-
ments with a view to strengthening their implementation. The gap report will be
considered by an ad hoc open‐ended working group to discuss options to address
the possible gaps. In this article, we reflect on the likely impact of this initial gap
identification and analysis phase of the intergovernmental process. We are specific-
ally concerned with the notion and the nature of ‘gaps’ in the context of the draft
Global Pact, the Resolution and more generally in IEL, and will explore whether the
concept of ‘gaps’ has meaningful value and whether such gaps are factual, technical
or normative in nature. While we believe an analysis of the strengths and weak-
nesses of IEL should be welcomed, we are not entirely convinced, however, that a
gap analysis in the form and fashion currently proposed is the most effective or use-
ful way to go about this.
1
|
INTRODUCTION
A key feature of the 2018 United Nations General Assembly (UNGA)
Resolution ‘Towards a Global Pact for the Environment’1 – the history,
content and purpose of which is described in greater detail here2 and
elsewhere in this special issue – is the preparation of a ‘technical and
evidence‐based’ report by the United Nations (UN) Secretary‐General
‘that identifies and assesses possible gaps in international environmental
law and environment‐related instruments with a view to strengthening
their implementation’.3 Such a report is to be considered by the ad hoc
open‐ended working group established under the Resolution, to
‘discuss possible options to address possible gaps … and, if deemed
necessary, the scope, parameters and feasibility of an international
instrument’.4 The gap assessment is a critical first phase in the formal
UN process that may or may not lead to the eventual adoption of ‘an
international instrument’. If adopted, informed as such an adoption
presumably would be by the gap analysis, the ambitions of the Pact's
earliest proponents might very well be fulfilled in due course, namely:
(i) to have a globally binding international environmental law (IEL)
instrument that (ii) entrenches all the major principles of IEL in one
document; whilst also (iii) developing the law progressively to provide
a globally recognized right to live in an ecologically sound environ-
ment, with associated procedural environmental rights.5
The process of conducting an ex ante gap analysis seems to be
gaining traction in global environmental politics, with the future

1

development of the Pact and possibly of other future multilateral
environmental agreements (MEAs) hinging on such a gap analysis
being conducted well before the negotiation process commences. The
norm‐creation process in the global environmental governance domain
is not entirely unfamiliar with the need to identify (and consequently
to fill) perceived gaps in IEL. Even as far back as 1995, the Interna-
tional Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Draft International
Covenant on Environment and Development (like the Global Pact) was
intended to become ‘an international legal instrument of general
scope, addressing the whole field of environment and development’;6
in other words, a document that would ‘fill in gaps in international law,
by placing in a global context principles which only appear in certain
places and by adding matters which are of fundamental importance
but which are not in any universal treaty’.7
Building on recent critique of the Global Pact's draft text, in the
present article we reflect on the likely impact of this initial gap identifi-
cation and analysis phase of the UN‐driven intergovernmental process.8
Importantly, conscious of the fact that the release of the gap report
coincided with the acceptance of this article for publication,9 it is not
the purpose of this article to consider possible gaps in the draft Global
Pact; or in a ‘technical’ manner the many potential gaps in IEL and the
manner in which the envisaged gap report might recommend how they
could or should be ‘assessed’;10 or even how the implementation of IEL
instruments could be ‘strengthened’ in the light of prevailing gaps.
While these are all pertinent and interesting points of analysis, we are
more concerned with the notion and the nature of ‘gaps’ in the specific
context of the Global Pact, and more generally in IEL, which we aim to
interrogate in this article. In doing so, we will raise a not inconsiderable
number of generic questions that are relevant for the broader field of
IEL, the answers to which are not immediately forthcoming.
The notion of a ‘gap’ in IEL – as in most areas of international law –
is an idea which, though easily understood at a linguistic level, raises
fundamental complexities conceptually. We will set to one side for the
moment the fact that the Resolution refers to ‘possible gaps’ as a
necessary textual ambiguity to ensure as broad an endorsement as
possible, though it does highlight the invariably contestable nature of
the objectivity of a gap, which we will consider below. Rather, we start
from the premise that as the Resolution refers to gaps in IEL, it is
appropriate to consider this matter from a legal perspective. But say-
ing this is a legal question does not get us too far, as the notion of a
gap is open‐ended and could – and probably does – embrace a wide
range of possible types of gaps. We identify three types for our
present purposes (there may be others): factual, technical and norma-
tive (rules and principles) gaps. There are, of course, significant over-
laps among these different types of gaps – specifically, that a factual
gap might invariably lead one to the conclusion of a concurrent and
synergistic normative gap – but each is also quite distinct. The wording
of the Resolution makes it possible for each type of gap sensibly to be
included in a gap analysis, though it is perhaps less likely that they will
be strictly categorized in this way in the light of the intergovernmental
audience receiving the report.
In reflecting on the notion and nature of the three types of gaps in
IEL that we have identified, the article will explore whether the con-
cept of ‘gaps’ has significant value, whether such gaps are factual,
technical or normative in nature, and what in fact such terms mean.
The article will suggest that the wording of the UNGA Resolution on
this matter is simultaneously progressive and conceptually incoherent,
the connection of the identification of gaps with ‘their implementation’
presumably referring to IEL and environment‐related instruments and
not to the gaps themselves. We further suggest that if the current
business‐as‐usual content of the draft Pact is anything to go by,11 even
if the gap report does identify gaps in IEL, they will not include – if for
no other reason than political acceptability – those necessary to
future‐proof a Global Pact (on the assumption that the report is not of
a defensive ontology to allow the working group to foreclose simply
the need for a Global Pact,12 but rather to feed into potential future
intergovernmental negotiations). The normative ‘gaps’ will most
probably not be of the more radical, creative type that are beginning
to find expression in certain areas of environmental law and policy
(e.g. the rights of nature),13 but as yet remain outside the primary dis-
course and principal binding instruments of IEL. Just like the famous
1960 English obscenity trial of the novel Lady Chatterley's Lover, what
was considered previously as radical, extreme or in that case obscene,
is now an accepted part of the canon. And we suggest that some of
those normative ‘gaps’ which we identify, though presently perceived
as unmentionable in mainstream debate,14 might very well also
become acceptable, and accepted, in future. In fact, they need to be
so, both for the long‐term integrity of IEL and, more importantly, for
long‐term Earth system integrity.

FACTUAL GAPS
Factual gaps are gaps in the coverage of IEL on matters that arguably
should be regulated. In many ways, identifying a factual gap is the first
stage of ascertaining whether there is a normative gap, though the
two are distinct; one might be prepared to accept a problem, but
whether it requires a legal response (as compared to a technological
solution, or simply changes in market or consumer preferences) is a
secondary and altogether very different consideration. The present
debate on tackling marine plastic pollution would seem to be a good
example of a factual gap, if only because there is widespread if not uni-
versal agreement that something must be done;15 but whether that
something must include a legal response is perhaps more arguable. Of
course, there are already established basic rules on marine pollution,
which provide a broad, outer framework of general rules.16 But is the
existence of certain generalized framework rules sufficient to say that
there is still a gap, be that factual or normative? Certainly, there is a
general view that the most effective form of international environ-
mental regulation is the adoption of detailed rules, occurring within
specific treaty regimes. General principles and overarching norms are
rarely regarded as an adequate substitute, although they could usefully
provide an enabling framework for further regulation. An example of
such an approach bearing fruit was the rapid adoption of highly
detailed rules on protecting the ozone layer, a regulatory concern in
which IEL has played a decisive role in addressing effectively.17 When
compared with the ozone regime, it would not seem difficult to argue
that there is a gap in the current law as regards marine plastic pollu-
tion. (Although admittedly, what also assisted with tackling the ozone
issue were changes in producer behaviour, prompted in part by law,
but also by the economics of greater consumer information). We will
return to this example below as regards normative gaps.
Nevertheless, not all issues have secured a sufficient global con-
sensus to say that there is a factual gap and as a consequence, a press-
ing need to regulate these concerns through detailed IEL regimes.
Take for instance environmental space debris, animal welfare and
hydraulic fracturing. While many scholars regard these as being critical
concerns warranting global regulation in their own right,18 there does
not (yet) seem to be sufficient political consensus on whether these
are ‘environmental problems’ requiring international regulation, or
even if they are, the nature and form that such international regulation
should take. And what of areas that are only partially regulated such as
genetically modified organisms, illegal logging and the stabilization of
greenhouse gases at 1.5°C above pre‐industrial levels?19
Are these
factual gaps or ‘covered’ matters with partial regulation as a result of
political contention? As noted above, the concept of a gap might
assume an objectivity, but this is invariably false: being able to ascer-
tain factual gaps is inherently a selective and therefore subjective exer-
cise, however conscientiously undertaken. Moreover, what of gaps
that we do not yet appreciate – the ‘known unknowns’ and ‘unknown
unknowns’ which former United States Secretary of Defense, Donald
Rumsfeld, once remarked upon;20 in this case, the damage that we are
doing to the Earth system that we either do not fully appreciate or that
we do not yet realize we are causing. They are, by definition, factual
gaps and yet they are of an order fundamentally different from the
other factual gaps identified above. One might tentatively also refer
here to those lesser well‐known, and therefore publicly far less preva-
lent, planetary boundaries, such as biogeochemical (nitrogen and phos-
phorus) flows to the biosphere and oceans;21 the damage to which,
we are told, are hugely destructive to the global environment. And yet
our understanding of these matters is arguably not as detailed as it is
now, for instance, on climate change. If there is a normative gap, it is
preceded very notably by a factual one; we simply either do not appre-
ciate the risks sufficiently or we are not yet prepared politically to act
accordingly.
3
|
TECHNICAL GAPS
The second type of gap is technical, which we interpret here with ref-
erence to the Resolution's clear link in its language to ‘strengthening
[their] implementation’. Noting the comment already made that the
implementation here must textually refer to IEL and environment‐
related instruments, and not to the gaps themselves, it nevertheless
raises a number of important queries about the purpose of identifying
the gaps and then as the Resolution says, for the ad hoc open‐ended
working group to ‘discuss possible options to address possible gaps’.
Technical gaps therefore relate to implementation as broadly under-
stood; in other words, how to make IEL more effective. As the Rus-
sian Federation argued in the UNGA debate prior to the adoption of
the Resolution, the focus should be on financing and implementation,
rather than on establishing new instruments.22 There is undoubtedly

a gap between the obligations States assume and full implementation;
and there is an even larger gap between those obligations, the pre-
sent state of the environment and the desired level of protection that
is critically required. The fact that the Resolution expressly mentions
‘implementation’ would thus firmly place these conversations within
the ambit of the ad hoc open‐ended working group's inquiry.
Politically, the issue of implementation goes to the heart of the
IEL debate: do we really need more norms or more instruments that
some view as leading to treaty congestion?23 Moreover, would a
focus on normative expansion not exacerbate the ‘fragmentation’ of
global environmental law and governance regimes, thus counterpro-
ductively undermining a key concern the drafters imagined the Glo-
bal Pact must tackle, that is, ‘strengthen the coherence of global
governance of the environment, currently characterized by the frag-
mentation of international institutions and the multiplication of inter-
national environmental norms both technical and sectoral’?24 Should
we not focus on better implementation instead? Seen in this light
therefore, the wording of the Resolution is a continuation of a long‐
standing debate.25 It also has strong North–South dimensions, when
reflecting the persistent relevance of common but differentiated
responsibilities and respective capabilities in IEL.26
There is also a second (related, but discrete) aspect to the notion of
technical gaps. That is, the existence of gaps in the technical, scientific
and socio‐economic data which underpin the functioning of such
regimes, and the full understanding of environmental challenges to
allow for more strategic, focused and sufficiently accommodative norm
development (and subsequent refinement), as well as for better imple-
mentation eventually. Are these gaps also within the scope of the Reso-
lution? They certainly connect to the core mandate of seeking to
strengthen implementation and would fit within the general tenor of
many States’ concerns that (regardless of the value of a new instru-
ment) implementation remains a particular issue within IEL.27 But just
as in the discussion of more traditional implementation gaps in the
paragraph above, identifying such gaps is one thing, while assessing
them is quite another. To mention but one example, this would be the
case for gaps arising from technology transfer.28 Will a gap report be
able to move a debate that has frustrated negotiators across numerous
regimes, spanning numerous decades? Most likely not. Is there a danger
that, intentionally or not, the gap report will be caught in, or even
worse, seek to prejudge, high‐level politics, where the only results are
empty platitudes? Hopefully not. But even if the report touches on
those matters that are generally agreed as being ongoing political dis-
agreements (i.e. ‘gaps’ in need of further political elaboration), such as
technology transfer at the global level, that will still take more political
will and considerable resources to correct than has so far proved possi-
ble. There remains a real risk of limited success based on past evidence.
4
|
NORMATIVE GAPS IN RELATION TO
RULES AND PRINCIPLES
The third type of gap is normative in nature. These gaps concern omit-
ted – as in some way non‐extant – rules and principles. It would seem
inevitable that a gap report would include such gaps as its principal pur-
pose if, as noted above, it is not to foreclose the possibility of the nego-
tiation and adoption of the Global Pact, but instead to inform the next
stages in the intergovernmental process, possibly towards the adoption
of a legally binding Global Pact. Nevertheless, ascertaining a normative
gap possibly is as difficult to conceptualize as any other type of gap. To
raise only some issues: How does one go about identifying normative
gaps in IEL? What is the methodology? Simply to ask whether there are
rules which the international community needs, but does not yet have,
seems innately subjective. To pick up again the example of marine plas-
tic pollution we raised above: is there a need for new rules? There are
some generalized norms which might be used, but have not as yet been
expressly clarified to tackle the issue specifically.29 Is that a normative
gap in IEL? And when discussing IEL rules, is it appropriate to talk about
gaps where treaty‐based rules actually exist but are of a regional
nature, so that there is no global coverage? Or where there is an MEA,
but it includes provisions that a State cannot accept on the basis of
their being too progressive, or insufficiently progressive? Again, is that
a normative gap in IEL? Are gaps containing soft law provisions (yet to
be translated into binding treaty law) still gaps because they apply to an
area that binding IEL does not regulate? In other words, does the fact
of their being non‐binding soft law result in a normative gap? And what
about those documents that exist in the legal–political space of norma-
tive desiderata? Examples might be the provisionally adopted 2018
International Law Commission's (ILC) first reading draft guidelines on
the protection of the atmosphere30 and the 2006 ILC draft principles
on the allocation of loss in the case of transboundary harm arising out
of hazardous activities,31 recognizing both the iterative status such ILC
documents can often have for a prolonged period of time, and the

FRENCH AND KOTZÉ

contested mix of codification and progressive development that they
sometimes contain.32 Is their normative ambiguity a gap in IEL? And
what of customary IEL rules? How should one interpret the Interna-
tional Court of Justice's (ICJ) determination in Pulp Mills on the River
Uruguay, that whilst undertaking an environmental impact assessment
in the face of the risk of transboundary harm is obligatory under IEL
(was there a gap before the judgment one must even ask?) more specif-
ically, ‘general international law [does not] specify the scope and con-
tent of an environmental impact assessment’.33 Thus, in terms of
substance, is such a view a deference to national law or a gap in IEL?
Moreover, as IEL remains on the whole voluntarist in nature, when
viewed at the level of individual States, a gap for one State (because it
is not party to a treaty or is a persistent objector to a rule of customary
international law) is not the same for another. But that of course is not
how ‘gaps’ in international law work; one usually talks of gaps in a sys-
tem, not of differences in individual obligations. On the other hand, we
might accept that variations in the extent to which regional legal
regimes cover IEL could constitute gaps (some regions for instance
have not yet adopted rules on access to environmental information
and environmental democracy);34 but variations between State partici-
pation in MEAs cannot be described as ‘gaps’; they are something for
States to work towards. Curiously, then, the UNGA Resolution has
done more than most documents to reinforce the idea of IEL as a sys-
tem, recognizing at a high level the very possibility of gaps, the implica-
tion being the existence of a putative whole in which normative
omissions exist. Whether the report it has asked for can identify nor-
mative gaps in that system is less clear. One begins to realize the
nuances in what would appear to be, on the face of it, a rather simple
question. What clearly emerges as an interim conclusion is that the
more one reflects on these questions, the less clear they become.
Identifying ‘gaps’ in the draft Pact, which arose from a non‐UN
process, is not the mandate for the UN Secretary General's gap
report, which is noticeably disconnected from the draft Global Pact
and referenced only obliquely in the Resolution.35 In other words,
the gap report is not intended to be a corrective for a ‘first‐version’
Global Pact. But while the gap analysis does not focus on the text of
the draft Pact, the Pact in its present form is not entirely excluded
from the gap analysis process; if only as a matter of its being
implicated in the design and content of whatever future vision
States would like to have of IEL. To this end, if the Global Pact is
the first iteration of what could become a universally binding instru-
ment of IEL which must, in the words of its drafters, ‘enshrine the
founding principles of environmental law’,36 then one must ask
whether the current proposed law is adequate and whether it con-
tains normative ‘gaps’. We focus on only three issues for our present
purposes.
First, setting aside for the moment the issue of whether the draft
Pact
ambitiously
manages
to
provide
the

for
Lex
Anthropocenae (a matter we focus on below), generally speaking does
the type of existing – or ‘founding’ and legally binding – norms it
reproduces set the desired standard of behaviour? Is ‘harm’ suffi-
ciently well‐defined? Does the norm provide too many exceptions or
is the differentiation it permits for different types of States (devel-
oped versus developing) too (in)flexible? Is it an obligation of con-
duct or of result? Of the many rules and principles included in the
draft Global Pact, there is a general sense that they are only broadly
scoped, and as we and others have argued, often insufficiently.37
One example is the draft Pact's treatment of equity. Draft Article 4
sets out the duty to observe and ensure intergenerational equity,
but it curiously does not provide for the critical issue of intragenera-
tional equity at a time when there are clear North–South inequalities
between people.38 The issue of intra‐species equity is also ignored,
which is surprising considering that many pervasive socio‐ecological
injustices abound not only between human beings of this and the
next generation, but also between human and non‐human entities of
this and the next generation. Other equity‐related principles such as
the equitable use of shared or common natural resources, and com-
mon responsibility for collective interests and goods including com-
mon areas, common heritage and common concern, have also not
been included.39 The draft Pact's view of equity is therefore decid-
edly narrow and exclusionary, and it is far from being comprehensive
in any meaningful sense. Other examples are those rules/principles
which have seen significant judicial elaboration over the past two
decades such as the prevention of harm, the precautionary principle,
environmental impact assessment and the remediation of environ-
mental harm. They are at present only cursorily sketched in the draft
Global Pact.40 Could we say that these principles are gaps if they
are merely regurgitated in their present narrowly circumscribed
form? Such omissions from the text may be gaps in a linguistic sense
(i.e. as having not been fully fleshed out), but they are arguably nei-
ther gaps in either the common usage of that term (because they are

rule as well as they could or should have). Simply put, though one
might take issue with the selective drafting of the draft Global Pact
– the reasons for which may be political and design‐driven for rea-
sons of space and ‘neatness’, or even perceived difficulties to cap-
ture fully the entirety of a rule – these are probably not gaps per se.
A second issue which is worth considering at this point is IEL's con-
tinued use and misuse of rules and principles as key terms in a wider
menagerie of concepts to describe both hard law (treaty and custom-
ary), soft law commitments and guidelines, decisions of MEA confer-
ences of the parties, as well as policy‐oriented actions. The literature
on rules and principles is vast,41 and unnecessary to summarize here.
But in relation to the concept of a normative gap, the difference in
normative status becomes increasingly stark and perhaps of greater
interest. When one talks of a normative gap, is one referring to binding
law only or to a wider range of forms, including general principles, soft
law texts and ideas de lege ferenda? Much will depend on one's view of
the international legal system, as to what constitutes law, and thus
whether one can validly, from an ontological basis, identify ‘gaps’ in
the law.42 There has been much discussion in international law as to
whether it is a closed system (in which case it is impossible for gaps to
exist in it) – largely premised around the Lotus presumption that what
is not proscribed is permitted43 – whether it is a complete system,
which whilst admitting of lacunae also admits of methodological
approaches to allow for their avoidance,44 or whether, rather, interna-
tional law should be viewed more as an open system, accepting that
the law might simply be silent on certain matters. On this last point, it
is what Bruno Simma, in his judicial role, once noted as ‘[t]he neutrality
of international law … [which] simply suggests that there are areas
where international law has not yet come to regulate, or indeed, will
never come to regulate’.45
Much of the literature on the issue of gaps in international law
has admittedly focused on the judicial response to such perceived
gaps,46 and yet a link invariably must exist between the (significant,
but arguably narrow) role of judicial gap‐filling and the systemic
development of international law, more generally, through State
practice and treaty negotiation. The specific purpose of this article
precludes a full analysis of this debate. Nevertheless, the nihilism
inherent in the Lotus presumption induces us to adopt a general
position that regardless of the jurisprudential debate on whether to
perceive international law as either a complete or an open system,
seeing the system as fully closed, must be – if only from an ethical
perspective – manifestly incorrect. As Melling says:
The utilisation of a ‘residual negative principle’ … [re-
ferred to above as the Lotus presumption] … to com-
plete the system does a disservice to the development of
international law as a coherent body of law … where a
gap in the law exists, the utilisation of a ‘residual nega-
tive principle’ does nothing to remedy the material gap
in the law and thereby contributes nothing to the devel-
opment of the law. It could be said that such an
approach
merely
entrenches
the
gap
and
arguably
obstructs the development of law.47
On a matter such as IEL (as in other areas of international law
which require a global, communitarian effort, such as human rights),
where the erga omnes nature of the interest is paramount, acceding to
the view that what is not prohibited is, by law, permitted – if it were
ever tenable48 – is contemporaneously unsustainable as a meta‐
principle either to guide ‘neighbourly’ State behaviour or to prompt
effective regulatory design. For environmental law, to accept the Lotus
presumption would be to ignore the many challenges thrown up by a
possible new geological epoch that is characterized by fundamental,
continuing and wide‐ranging Earth system changes. The Anthropocene
arguably demands a level of normative ambition,49 or a global environ-
mental constitutional moment, similar to the one last seen with the
creation of the United Nations in 1945 and the adoption of the
Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948:
The world saw a major transformative shift in govern-
ance after 1945 that led to the establishment of the UN
and numerous other international organizations, along
with far-reaching new international legal norms on
human rights and economic cooperation. We need simi-
lar changes today, a ‘constitutional moment’ in world
politics and global governance.50
It is in the light of this need for progressive development that
we, third and finally, need to consider those rules and principles
which have not yet been agreed by the international community.

These are similar to but distinct from the normative gaps discussed
above. They are more aspirational and certainly radical in nature,
reflecting a genesis that originates instead from other sources:
jurisprudence, philosophical and ethical approaches to environmental
care, alternatives to the mainstream, religious doctrine or simply new
ideas. These are the ‘unmentionable gaps’ as they are not yet, or not
ordinarily, part of the mainstream (international law) discourse – or,
if included, invariably in a preambular manner. Some examples are
the rights of nature, ecological democracy, Earth system governance
and law, Earth system integrity, the principle of in dubio pro natura
and the ecological rule of law, all of which have the potential to
push for a radically different and more ambitious normative frame-
work, to address the systemic challenges inherent in IEL and global
environmental governance, and to increase the normative reach,
power and impact of norms that must ultimately seek to counter the
socio‐economic–political–juridical system's neoliberal anthropocen-
trism and exploitation of the Earth system.51 Some of these already
exist in domestic laws and even in non‐binding international instru-
ments such as the World Charter for Nature of 1982, and they have
significant potential to form the basis of a new legal paradigm for
the Anthropocene, or Lex Anthropocenae; the exact outlines and con-
tent of which are still unclear.52
Importantly though, these radical provisions are not present in
the draft Global Pact; a critical concern that, starting with the gap
analysis, could be addressed in order to future‐proof, as it were, the
Global Pact (and indeed IEL) through the eventual incorporation of
such radical and creative provisions. What would be the purpose of
a gap report in this context? To strengthen and future‐proof any
new IEL instrument or merely to improve what already exists? We
certainly consider that the Resolution, and the legal reform process
that might follow its gap analysis, present the international commu-
nity with an important opportunity to adopt such radical provisions
in a globally binding instrument. But for this to happen, strategically,
a gap report must validly include such discussion within its mandate
of ‘identif[ying] … possible gaps in international environmental law’.
In other words, it must challenge States to rise above their own ter-
ritorial and self‐interested short‐termist and anthropocentric consid-
erations and instead to adopt an Earth system perspective that at
once also offers a normatively ambitious and radically different legal
paradigm for the Anthropocene. Politically, of course, such reports
rarely do this; they are simply not given the scope. As this is a UN
Secretary‐General report, it is independently drafted but perhaps less
capable of being as substantively radical as, for instance, a UN Spe-
cial Rapporteur's report. Indeed, the explicit reference to the gap
report's being ‘technical and evidence‐based’ would seem to have
specifically circumscribed any approach other than a limited analysis.
To the extent that the draft Global Pact could be an indication
of what we might expect a future binding instrument of IEL to
look like, informed as such a future instrument will also presumably
be by the gap analysis, there is considerable reason to believe that
future reform processes of IEL and possibly the gap report that
must initiate such reforms will be equally unambitious. After all,
the Pact was drafted outside of the formal UN processes by a
Group of Experts53 which had considerable freedom of imagination
and creativity and was essentially unconstrained by the stifling
limits and limitations presented by State sovereignty, the neoliberal
economic growth agenda and the many pitfalls of realpolitik, now
ever more evident in a world characterized by post‐truth politics,
extremist populism, eco‐crisis denialism, radical anti‐rationalism, and
a rejection of rational science and the rule of law.54 Not even this
Group of Experts managed to push the envelope by being innova-
tive and normatively ambitious. States on the other hand are sub-
ject to these constraints and it is highly unlikely they will raise the
bar in any future negotiation efforts to address the ‘unmentionable
gaps’ in IEL. In fact, States might never even have the chance to
embark on such fundamental reforms, since the gap report itself
might avoid mentioning the ‘unmentionable gaps’ in IEL and might
avoid recommending that they be addressed by the international
community. In other words, the report itself risks creating a ‘chil-
ling’ effect, premised on a negative cyclical assumption that what
States do not want to hear, they should not in any case receive. If
this is the case, the gap report will be a disappointment to those
who, like us, appreciate the critical need for starting to develop a
more radical Lex Anthropocenae.

CONCLUSION
In this article, we have endeavoured to reflect on the issue of gaps
in IEL, an inquiry that we have situated within the context of the
draft Global Pact and the UNGA‐mandated gap analysis that has
been initiated. Generally speaking, we believe an analysis of the
strengths and weaknesses of IEL should be welcomed to the extent
that it might provide a foundation to pursue reforms of IEL; reforms
which we are of the view are critically needed in the Anthropocene.
We are not entirely convinced, however, that an analysis of gaps in
the form and fashion proposed by the UNGA Resolution is the most
effective or useful way to go about this.
We agree with Bodansky that what he calls ‘descriptive gaps’ will be
difficult to assess. Descriptive gaps – not altogether dissimilar from our
technical and factual characterization of gaps – are simply ‘discontinu
it[ies]’; they are non liquets which exist ‘if at all, only in very rare cases
where the law does not decide an issue one way or the other – where
an action is neither permitted nor prohibited’.55 On the other hand,
